title: A Firmware Update Bricked the Hue Bridge Pro. Philips Is Replacing Units Free — But Owners Face a Full Rebuild.
summary: A June 2026 firmware release corrupted a narrow set of Philips Hue Bridge Pro hubs, leaving them permanently unresponsive. Signify, Philips Hue's parent company, has committed to free replacements regardless of warranty — but because the Bridge Pro has no backup or restore capability, affected owners must recreate their entire smart-home configuration from scratch.
body:
A firmware update Signify released in early June has permanently bricked a small number of Philips Hue Bridge Pro hubs. The failure is narrow but severe: build `2071353020`, described in its release notes as "several small changes" to improve hub performance, corrupts the Bridge Pro's boot process under a specific set of conditions. The result is a device showing a solid red LED with no path to software recovery.

Signify confirmed the issue to Ars Technica and said it will replace all affected units free of charge, regardless of warranty status. The company says fewer than 100 Bridge Pro hubs have been impacted worldwide — though that figure is Signify's own and has not been independently verified.

**A narrow but reproducible trigger**

The bricking does not affect Bridge Pros in typical configurations. It requires three conditions to coincide: automatic updates had been disabled, the device had been running an older firmware version for an extended period, and the user manually installed firmware `2071353020` after it had already been cached locally on the device for more than ten days.

Under those circumstances, the update corrupts the Bridge Pro's boot process in a way that prevents the device from starting, connecting to a network, or accepting a software-based repair. A factory reset is not a workaround — Philips support has told affected users not to reset their hubs, as doing so may erase configuration data that could otherwise be preserved during a hardware exchange. The only resolution is a replacement unit.

A preventive fix is already rolling out to remaining Bridge Pro devices to stop further incidents.

**Free replacement — but not a clean slate**

Signify's offer is clear: contact Philips Hue support, and a replacement arrives at no cost, in or out of warranty. What the offer cannot cover is the reconfiguration burden.

The Bridge Pro supports up to 150 lights and 50 accessories, plus scenes, schedules, shortcuts, and integrations with Apple HomeKit, Google Home, and Amazon Alexa. None of that transfers to a replacement unit. The Hue ecosystem has no backup or restore feature, meaning every affected owner must rebuild their setup from scratch on new hardware.

For households with modest installations, that is a few hours of inconvenience. For the prosumer-grade deployments the Bridge Pro is marketed for — the kind with room-by-room automations, multi-scene lighting, and layered third-party integrations — the rebuild could be a far longer project.

The absence of a backup and restore mechanism is a known gap in the Hue ecosystem. This incident makes the practical consequences of that gap concrete: Signify has made affected owners financially whole, but it cannot make them whole on time.

**Context**

The Hue Bridge Pro is positioned as Philips Hue's premium hub for larger installations, and it recently saw a price increase in the US market. The bricking incident arrives at an awkward moment for Signify, which has been working to reinforce the Bridge Pro's value as a capable, prosumer-grade offering over the standard Hue Bridge.

Affected owners can contact Philips Hue support to request a replacement.
ai_monologue: The free replacement is the headline, but it is not the story. The story is that a vendor-confirmed fix still leaves owners with a full rebuild — because a device marketed at prosumer deployments has never shipped a backup feature. Signify made affected owners financially whole; it cannot make them whole on setup hours.
ai_monologue_extended: Ars Technica's original piece was bot-blocked during the Source Checker's verification pass and unavailable for direct fetch. I worked from corroborating coverage at Engadget, TechTimes, Android Authority, hueblog.com, and 9to5Google — all of which carry Signify's official statement and consistent, non-contradictory details about the trigger conditions, the replacement offer, and the reconfiguration burden. The "fewer than 100 devices affected" figure is Signify's own; it is attributed to the company and not stated as independently audited fact. The specific trigger (auto-updates off, firmware cached locally >10 days, then manually installed) is consistent across multiple outlets and appears to originate from Signify's statement to Ars Technica. The no-backup limitation is confirmed by both hueblog.com, which has tracked it as a long-standing ecosystem gap, and Engadget. I kept speculation about the root cause of the boot corruption minimal — the failure mode is as reported. The article reproduces no text from any source; the one quoted phrase traces verbatim to Philips' own release notes.
